DSAAT: Dual-Space Adaptive Adversarial Training for Robust Network Intrusion Detection

PDF
Shuijun Yin; Junzhe Cai; Yuqing Huang

Abstract:

Deep learning-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) are highly effective yet vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which can be launched in either the feature space or the problem (raw traffic) space. Existing adversarial training defenses often suffer from limited attack diversity and a narrow focus on a single attack space, leaving systems exposed to cross-space cooperative threats. To address these limitations, we first investigate adversarial domain constraints—specifically, how to impose feature-level mutability, range, and dependency restrictions to enable the generation of protocol-compliant adversarial network traffic in the problem space. Building upon this foundation, we propose Dual-Space Adaptive Adversarial Training (DSAAT), a reinforcement learning-driven framework that dynamically generates diverse and semantically valid adversarial examples across both feature and problem spaces. This closedloop interaction between an adaptive strategy generator and the NIDS enables the model to learn robust decision boundaries without being overwhelmed by redundant or invalid samples. Evaluated on the CIC-IDS2017 dataset against six state-of-the-art attack methods, DSAAT achieves an average adversarial accuracy of 91.16% while maintaining near-perfect clean-sample detection performance, significantly outperforming existing baselines.

I. Introduction

As network-traffic threats continue to intensify, network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) based on traffic analysis offer substantial research significance and practical potential [1]–[3]. By monitoring and analyzing network traffic in real time, NIDS can detect anomalous behaviors and attack patterns, providing timely alerts and support for cyber defense. Despite the strong performance of deep-learning-based NIDS in malicious traffic detection, their effectiveness is challenged by the intrinsic fragility of neural networks, which makes them vulnerable to adversarial examples [4], [5].
